Verified batch-compilation of agent-initiated bulk operations: prove a synthesized (or agent-declared) batch's write-set stays inside the envelope and transactionally checkpoint its execution before committing, rather than trusting either manual per-item repetition or an unverified ad hoc script. Keep this even if the anti-unification detector never works — an agent can simply declare 'I'm about to do this N times' and the durable contribution is proving the blast radius before it runs, not the detector that finds the pattern.

attacks: Missing plan-level checkpoint (undisclosed regression, not a listed limitation): PORTCULLIS has ONLY per-action warrant checking against a generic Constitution — no plan-time proof that the trajectory as a whole is sound. This repo's own openDaisugi (ADR-0007) built call-time gating and deliberately kept it as a SECOND checkpoint 'beside plan verification, never a replacement,' stating: 'A call being inside the envelope does not make the trajectory benign; individually-admitted calls can compose into harm.' PORTCULLIS silently drops that half of the architecture and it does not appear in its own 7-item failureModes list — a real regression from the design it's descended from, presented as complete.

Rollback restores disk state, not conversation state — the flagship transactional-substrate claim is a category error. 'An in-workspace mistake costs a rollback, not a token-burning recovery arc' doesn't follow: CoW snapshots undo the filesystem, but the wrong action, its output, and the rejection/rollback event all remain in the transcript. The agent still has to notice, diagnose, and re-plan around it — that IS where recovery-arc tokens are spent. This kills the central saving claimed for M1/M3.

Net-token math inverts under the design's own adoption path: shadow mode. Input savings depend entirely on deleting standing policy prose because enforcement is 'structural, not textual.' But real gates ship shadow-by-default for adoption reasons — this repo's own ADR-0007 records enforce-by-default being overruled precisely because 'a gate nobody dares install protects nobody.' In shadow mode nothing is enforced, so the safe move is to KEEP the prose AND pay gate overhead: net negative for an unbounded startup period the roadmap never prices.

The generic ~20-invariant Constitution is priced like a moat but functions like a chroot. Task-specific envelopes are optional; the load-bearing common-case guarantee is workspace containment / no-egress, run through a full SMT refinement pipeline. A bind-mount, read-only root, and a blocked network namespace deliver most of that for free with no warrant vocabulary and no solver latency. The design never argues why the expensive path beats the cheap one for the case that dominates real traffic — the solver only earns its keep on the optional, rarer task-envelope path.

'A proxy the model physically cannot bypass' contradicts the design's own honesty section three fields later: failure mode #5 admits any unproxied tool is 'a total bypass' and the boundary must be 'exhaustively enumerated or the guarantee is theatre.' The sibling shipped hook-gate (ADR-0007) names concrete channels outside its control — the host's outer hook timeout, a harness that silently stops firing hooks, a block path that doesn't block. The core-mechanism claim overclaims certainty the design's own failure-mode list retracts.

The headline 10-100x batch-compilation number is generic 'write a script instead of doing it by hand' savings, not something attributable to the safety machinery — any competent coding agent already does this unprompted. The comparison baseline (214 manual agent turns) is a strawman; the honest comparison is PORTCULLIS's k-sample-dry-run-plus-monitor overhead against a plain script a capable agent would write anyway. The assurance wrapper is a correctness argument (catch a bad transform before it hits all 214 files), not the claimed multiplier.

Rare-hard-task coverage is real but narrow, and the framing claims more than it delivers. Mechanisms (a) and (b) only pay off when a task is hard because it's risky/destructive or internally repetitive. A rare task that's hard because it demands difficult reasoning or research, with no destructive action and no batch structure, gets zero benefit — no token savings, no correctness lift, pure pass-through. That's plausibly the modal 'rare hard task' and the design never names the gap.

Not novel relative to its own lineage: propose-then-verify, tighten-only envelopes (monotone narrowing), fail-closed, layer-not-harness, and even the exact 0%-to-30-59% Governance Decay citation are near-verbatim restatements of this repo's own shipped VISION.md / ADR-0003 / ADR-0004 / ADR-0007. What's actually new is a handful of bolt-ons of uneven value (daemon framing, CoW rollback, batch-program verification, counterfactual ledger), wrapped in a rebrand with freshly invented percentages.

Every quantitative claim (10-30% prefill, 25-35% output, 10-100x batch, 'roughly zero' overhead) is stated with no measurement methodology, corpus, or confidence interval — a precision level this design's own sibling project explicitly refuses to claim for itself ('the corpus is benchmark-generated, read it as what the ruler finds here'). PORTCULLIS asserts as settled fact what its own lineage treats as an open empirical question.
crits.buildability: Two-tier. The solver/envelope/tightening-proof core is proven buildable by a small team — it is already built and shipped in this repo's own openDaisugi codebase (Z3-backed verify, envelope_subsumes, ADR-0003 tightening, ~20k LOC / ~1750 tests). But M1 as scoped ('zero unmediated side effects on a red-team bypass suite,' 'the model physically cannot bypass') asks for total mediation across every filesystem/process/network boundary an agent could reach — closer in scope to building a sandboxing/virtualization layer than a milestone. The sibling project deliberately chose a lighter hook-based integration instead (ADR-0007) and candidly lists fail-open edges it does not control (host hook timeout, a harness that stops firing hooks, a block path that doesn't block); PORTCULLIS's M1 exit bar is stricter than what the team that already built this space judged achievable. Batch-program verification and the counterfactual ledger are moderate lifts mostly because they overlap existing pathway/distillation machinery already in the repo — that overlap is the real reason they're cheap, not novel engineering.
crits.compactionVerdict: The architectural claim is sound and the strongest part of the design: enforcement lives outside the token stream (an out-of-process gate, content-addressed envelopes), so it structurally cannot be summarized away — this matches the same Governance Decay citation and mechanism this repo's own openDaisugi already ships. But the design prices the win in isolation. Compaction still erases policy AWARENESS; the design's own fix is 'the exact violated clause re-enters context at clause-size cost' via reject-with-clause — a rejection-retry loop. The correctness win is bought by shifting cost onto the very token budget the design separately claims to shrink, and that transfer is never netted against the savings math.
keepIdeas: Per-instance counterfactual pricing: sealed-sandbox replay of the blocked/mechanism-off branch priced against the SAME instance rather than a benchmark average directly targets this repo's own admitted evidence gap ('the corpus is benchmark-generated ... point it at your own journal'). Keep the goal of per-instance, no-benchmark-needed measurement; drop the 'same-instance controlled experiment' framing, since LLM sampling nondeterminism means a post-divergence replay is not actually a controlled comparison — it's evidence, not proof, and should be labeled as such.

Verification-underwrites-aggressive-cheap-model-routing: bounding a cheap model's blast radius so it can be routed to far more often is a genuinely underexplored angle, distinct from the envelope/solver core, and composes cleanly with budget/sizing logic that already exists in this repo rather than being a repackaging of prior work.
crits.netTokenVerdict: Does not close as stated. Three concrete leaks: (1) shadow-mode operation — the real-world adoption path this exact lineage's own ADR-0007 chose — requires keeping the policy prose in context AND paying gate overhead simultaneously, a straightforward net-negative the roadmap never bounds in time; (2) the flagship transactional-rollback saving is a category error (disk state is not conversation state, so the claimed recovery-arc cost isn't actually removed, only the file-repair portion is); (3) the 10-100x batch-compilation number is generic scripting benefit misattributed to the safety layer rather than derived from it, and none of the input/output percentage estimates carry any stated measurement methodology.
crits.rareTaskVerdict: Real but narrow. Shape-based first-occurrence safety and internal-repetition batch compilation are genuine, history-independent mechanisms — not hand-waved for the subset of tasks that are hard because they're risky/destructive or mechanically repetitive. But the design offers nothing — and by its own 'safe-but-wrong gap' failure mode implicitly concedes it offers nothing — for a rare task that's hard because it demands difficult reasoning or research, with no destructive action and no batch structure. That case plausibly IS the modal rare-hard-task, and PORTCULLIS is inert on it: zero token savings, zero correctness lift, pure Tier-0 pass-through dressed in language that implies general applicability.
crits.steelman: If you accept the parent thesis this design is clearly descended from (an LLM proposes a checkable spec, a solver verifies actions stay inside it, verification lives outside the token stream so compaction can't erase it), PORTCULLIS's genuine contribution is pushing three of that thesis's edges further than the shipped version does — literal out-of-process mediation instead of a hook, transactional rollback for cheap in-workspace mistake recovery, and per-instance counterfactual pricing that answers the parent project's own admitted 'my corpus is synthetic' evidence gap.

attacks: Rare-hard-task bait-and-switch: the flagship '40-file task pays out on 37' example is a WIDE/repetitive task merely instantiated within one session, not the deep/singular/reasoning-heavy task 'rare hard' usually denotes (heisenbug, novel design, ambiguous negotiation). For those, k>=2-3 structural similarity never fires, and the design's own cold-start floor admits this contributes ~0.

The retry-spiral-aversion mechanism (claimed 15-40% output savings, the one lever that DOES generalize to deep hard tasks) is undercut by the design's own admitted 'semantic gap' failure mode: most retry spirals on hard tasks come from actions that are allowed-but-wrong (logic errors within scope), which the gate explicitly cannot catch. The magnitude claim and the failure-mode list contradict each other.

Compaction argument-validity failure, not just incompleteness: the design infers 'safe to compact aggressively' from 'policy authority is extra-contextual,' but policy-compliance was never the binding constraint on compaction aggressiveness -- task competence was. User intent, discovered facts, and implicit invariants ('match the existing test's semantics') live only in the transcript, are unexpressed in the predicate algebra, and are absent from the ledger (post-state digests, not rationale). The design rebuts a policy-shaped objection (the cited violation cliff) with policy-shaped evidence, then books a general-purpose compaction license the argument doesn't support.

Sample-validate-then-generalize reintroduces self-certification, contradicting the headline claim directly: the acceptance postcondition is LLM-authored, validated on 2-3 of N elements, then trusted for all N. That is a heuristic dressed as a correctness layer, and per-element rollback only fires on failures the same LLM-authored predicate is capable of detecting -- the exact self-certification loop the gate was built to avoid, reintroduced one layer up.

TOCTOU (on the design's own failure list) degrades the guarantee from proven to proven-at-verification-time specifically for irreversible acts (send/purchase/external POST) -- the highest-blast-radius class, where a stale snapshot check is a correctness failure, not a practicality footnote.

'Human-owned standing charter' is hollowed out by its own stated mitigation: 'shipped default charters per workspace archetype' means the operative permissive authority for most real deployments is vendor-authored and never read by the household/team it governs -- the monotone-narrowing law is airtight against the AGENT widening scope, but says nothing about a badly-scoped human-facing default.

Net-token math is evidentiarily asymmetric: the surveyor model call (task + workspace facts in, charter predicates out) is a real per-task cost never entered into savesMagnitude; gate/solver overhead is bounded only by an M2 ROADMAP TARGET ('<1% overhead'), not a measurement. 'Never negative ROI' is proven only for the narrowest case (zero side effects, no surveyor call) and oversold as universal -- a short, one-off, side-effecting, first-try-successful task pays full surveyor+gate cost and collects near-zero compilation or retry-spiral benefit.

Category error in the input-savings figure: the cited 30-70%/41-80% compaction range is the field's general compaction ceiling, not PACT's marginal contribution. PACT's real marginal contribution is the delta between compaction achievable unsafely (which cost-conscious teams may already take) and compaction achievable safely -- likely much smaller than the number booked.

M4 (structural-similarity loop detection + program synthesis from 2-3 examples + whole-parameter-space symbolic verification) is the least de-risked milestone yet the one the output-savings numbers depend on most; it's an open-ended program-synthesis problem given equal roadmap weight to four comparatively routine engineering milestones -- a planning red flag.

Composability is silent on sub-agent/parallel execution: the design's own TOCTOU fix requires 'one snapshot lock,' implying serialized gate access, a plausible throughput bottleneck for parallel sub-agents that the doc never addresses.
crits.rareTaskVerdict: Partially hand-waved. The only lever that truly requires zero task-recurrence (averted retry spirals) has its claimed magnitude undercut by the design's own admitted semantic gap. The lever with the concrete worked example (intra-instance compilation) actually depends on within-task repetition -- a narrower, easier-to-satisfy condition than genuine task rarity, smuggled in as if it answered the harder question. Genuinely deep, singular, reasoning-heavy hard tasks get: no compilation benefit (admitted), an input-side-only compaction benefit that may be offset by a lost-rationale re-derivation tax, and a retry-spiral benefit whose real magnitude is unclear once you subtract the allowed-but-wrong failure class the gate can't catch.
crits.compactionVerdict: Fails, not just incomplete. The claim conflates two different things: 'the enforcement mechanism survives compaction' (true and well-argued -- the charter/gate/ledger live outside the transcript, so there's nothing for compaction to drop on that axis) and 'correctness/safety survives compaction' (asserted but not supported -- policy-compliance was never what made compaction risky for task quality; the transcript's rationale, discovered facts, and unstated invariants are the load-bearing content compaction destroys, and none of that is protected by, or even visible to, the gate). Worse, the design's own logic licenses MORE aggressive compaction because the gate exists, which increases pressure on exactly the undefended axis. Additionally, sample-validate-then-generalize and CoW rollback are enrolled as correctness layers that also depend on transcript-resident LLM judgment, so the 'survives compaction' claim, read as covering the design's own stated correctness apparatus (not just the narrow gate), does not hold.
crits.netTokenVerdict: Does not clearly close. Savings are specific and ranged with citations to background research; new costs the design itself introduces (surveyor call, Tier-2/3 solver overhead, ledger rehydration) are left as roadmap targets rather than measurements -- an asymmetric evidentiary standard. The headline input-savings figure appears to book the field's general compaction ceiling rather than PACT's actual marginal contribution (the safety delta). 'Never negative ROI' is demonstrated only for the zero-side-effect case and likely false for short, one-off, side-effecting, first-try-successful tasks, which are common.
crits.buildability: Mixed, with a real research risk hiding inside an engineering-looking roadmap. M1/M2 (predicate algebra, SMT compilation, fail-closed gate) plausibly overlap substantially with prior shipped work referenced in this workspace's own history (a Z3-backed verifier, a call-time gate) -- treated here as a stated inference from repo/commit context, not a verified fact, and used only as a buildability credit, not a novelty penalty. M3 (compaction-event hooks) is harness-dependent and may not be cleanly exposable in third-party harnesses. M4 (intra-instance program synthesis from 2-3 examples over arbitrary tool-call sequences) is an open research problem given the same roadmap weight as routine milestones -- the flagship output-savings mechanism is the least de-risked part of the plan. Composes well with prompt caching and model routing (correctly identified architectural separations); silent on sub-agent parallelism, where its own single-snapshot-lock design implies serialization.
keepIdeas: The same-instance counterfactual meter (measured cost of the first k acts x (N-k) vs actual synthesis+verify+apply cost): the only piece of the design that makes its own savings claims falsifiable per-occurrence, with no benchmark or corpus needed -- worth keeping as a measurement discipline independent of whether the synthesis engine itself ever ships.

The narrow, defensible version of 'policy authority belongs outside the context window' -- as an enforcement-plane/working-memory-plane separation that makes the ALLOWED check compaction-proof by construction -- kept strictly separate from the overreaching inference that this also licenses aggressive compaction of task-relevant rationale, which it does not.
crits.steelman: PACT's one real contribution is cleanly separating "is this action allowed" (proven by a deterministic, extra-contextual gate whose authority a self-narrowing LLM can never widen) from "is this action right" (explicitly never claimed), which is a genuinely different move from prompt-based guardrails or RLHF-style alignment and is honest enough to name its own boundary.

Interlock's real bet is architectural, not procedural: by moving the permission check and the commit/rollback boundary into a sidecar keyed to deterministic state rather than to the transcript, it decouples "is this action allowed" from "does the model remember the rules," which is the one dependency that makes aggressive compaction and cheap-model routing unsafe today.
attacks: Rare-hard-task mechanism is real but much narrower than billed: of the four levers, only (1) checked macro-execution is a large win, and it fires only when a hard task ALSO happens to be internally repetitive/batchable — a specific intersection, not 'rare hard tasks' generally. On a genuinely novel, non-repetitive, low-failure-rate hard task, the design's own honest answer is '~zero' savings — cost-neutral scaffolding, not a cost reducer, which undercuts the headline claim.

'Net effect on success rate is non-negative by construction' is false as stated. The delta envelope is drafted by a separate model call with LESS context than the acting agent, and false positives (failure mode #1, over-tight envelopes) concentrate exactly on novel actions — the case mechanism (4) claims to serve. Blocking a legitimate action changes the trajectory, it doesn't pause it; the design treats an independent risk item (over-tight envelopes) as orthogonal to the payoff (routing) it actually undermines. The two are negatively correlated, not independent.

Counterfactual inflation on the flagship savings number: the 240-file macro-execution win (60-90% claimed) is measured against 'agent does 240 individual turns,' but any competent agent today already collapses that to 'write and test one script' with zero Interlock machinery. Against the TRUE baseline (naive batch scripting), Interlock's marginal contribution is safety-checking the script pre-commit — real, but a much smaller slice of the claimed number. Most of the headline saving isn't attributable to the novel parts of the architecture.

Rollback savings carry an unmetered input cost the design's own three meters never charge against them: after every rollback the agent must be re-told workspace state, what was attempted, and why it failed. N rollbacks = N x (ledger-prefill + re-derivation of situational awareness the agent already had before the rollback). Meter (c) counts only the avoided undo-REASONING (output side) and is silent on this rehydration tax (input side) — this is the concrete, load-bearing instance of 'injected specs/instructions can raise input more than they save output,' not a hypothetical.

The evaluation plan cannot verify the claim it exists to verify. M5's A/B harness 'replays a single recorded task with the layer on vs off' — but agent execution is stochastic, so the off-run diverges from the on-run at the first decision point, producing two different trajectories rather than a controlled counterfactual. A rare hard task is n=1 by definition, so there is no population to average over either. Every number in savesMagnitude is defined as 'metered against the counterfactual,' and for exactly the task class the rubric asks about, that counterfactual cannot be constructed by the design's own method — the rare-hard-task savings claim is structurally unfalsifiable, not merely optimistic.

Correctness/safety bundles two guarantees of very different strength under one name. ALLOWED-ness is mechanical, fail-closed, and genuinely survives compaction (a real strength). RIGHT-ness is explicitly NOT proven — it's bottlenecked by the task's own test coverage, i.e. exactly the same guarantee ordinary CI already gives, with no novel contribution. A reader who hears 'correctness guarantee survives compaction' will over-trust the rightness half, which the document itself disclaims only in a footnote-style failure mode ('semantic gap'). Monotonic tightening also doesn't prevent a delta that is tighter-than-floor yet semantically wrong for the task — that class of error is invisible to the monotonicity check.

Compaction safety is proven only for enforcement state, not for reasoning quality. The design correctly shows the floor/ledger survive compaction mechanically, then leaps to 'safe to compact aggressively' — but on hard tasks, success rate plausibly depends on retained deliberation (ruled-out hypotheses, dead ends, partial insights), none of which the ground-truth ledger preserves. Compacting that away on exactly the tasks where it matters most could increase total tokens via re-derivation, even though nothing becomes unsafe. The document never distinguishes 'safe to compact' from 'costless to compact.'

Escrow — the mechanism correctness and much of the cost story lean on — is only well-defined for reversible, locally-observable effects (filesystem, git, transactional DB). The design's own failure-mode list admits email sends, purchases, and external API POSTs can't be escrowed or rolled back, which routes them to human escalation. That's a large and growing share of real agent action space (web/browser agents, third-party API calls, computer use) where the flagship safety mechanism simply doesn't apply, and the document doesn't scope this prominently despite it gutting generality.

Buildability is uneven across milestones in a way the roadmap's flat 'weeks' cadence hides. M1 (floor + gate) is a genuinely small, buildable proxy — comparable to existing policy-as-code/seccomp-style wrappers, modest novelty. M2 (general escrow: shadow-run arbitrary shell/HTTP/browser actions, capture 'every path touched, every verb, every egress,' commit/rollback atomically) is adjacent to building a lightweight sandboxing/hypervisor layer (gVisor/Firecracker-class engineering) for heterogeneous, non-transactional tool surfaces — a multi-quarter-to-multi-year effort for a small team, not a milestone alongside M1's 'weeks.'

SMT-solving for 'path/glob/quota/ordering constraints' invokes more machinery than the stated problem needs — path-prefix and glob matching are decidable by ordinary pattern matching for the vast majority of real policies. Reaching for an SMT solver buys rigor-by-association while introducing a genuinely new failure mode (solver timeout -> fail-closed -> unattended-run stall) that a simpler algorithm wouldn't have.
crits.rareTaskVerdict: Not hand-waved as pure fiction — the cold-start story (floor active from action #1, no prior-trace dependency, lazy delta drafting) is a real and creditable design move that most learned/history-based cost systems lack. But the actual savings mechanisms attack execution OVERHEAD (retry cost, prefill cost, batch-turn collapse), not the intrinsic reasoning cost of solving a hard problem, and the one large lever (checked macro-execution) requires the hard task to also be structurally repetitive — a narrow intersection, not the general case. Worse, the design's own evaluation method (M5's on/off replay of a single recorded task) cannot produce a valid counterfactual for a stochastic, n=1, non-repetitive hard task: the off-run diverges at the first decision point. So the rare-hard-task claim is not just narrower than advertised, it is unverifiable by the design's own proposed method — a claim that can't be falsified isn't earning full marks as a mechanism.
crits.compactionVerdict: Enforcement (allowed-ness) survives compaction by architecture, not discipline — the floor, delta, and ledger live in sidecar process state evaluated per tool call regardless of transcript content, which is the design's strongest and most defensible claim. But two things are conflated under 'survives compaction': the SAFETY guarantee genuinely does; the SUCCESS-RATE benefit of aggressive compaction on hard tasks does not, because the ledger preserves ground-truth workspace state, not the deliberation trail (ruled-out approaches, partial insights) that hard-task performance may depend on. 'Safe to compact' is demonstrated; 'costless to compact' on hard tasks is asserted, not shown, and could go the other way (re-derivation of forgotten reasoning burning more tokens than compaction saves).
crits.netTokenVerdict: Doesn't close as a single aggregate claim because the three mechanisms have different, uncombinable token signatures and the overhead side is never metered symmetrically with the savings side. Macro-execution hits both input and output (fewer turns = less prefill and less generation) but its counterfactual baseline is inflated — measured against naive per-file turns rather than against 'agent already writes a batch script without Interlock,' so much of the claimed win isn't attributable to the novel machinery. Ledger-backed compaction is input-only savings and depends on reasoning-trace loss being harmless, which is unproven on hard tasks. Cheap rollback is output-positive (skips undo-reasoning) but input-negative in a way the design doesn't charge for: each rollback requires re-injecting ledger state plus re-deriving situational awareness the agent already had, and on a thrashing cheap-model retry loop this rehydration cost can exceed the undo-reasoning it replaced. The design meters savings in detail (three named meters) and treats overhead only qualitatively (as failure modes) — an asymmetric accounting that can't demonstrate closure either way.
crits.buildability: Bimodal. M1 (interposition shim + human-authored floor + fail-closed rejection + decision log) is small-team-buildable in the stated weeks and is close to existing policy-as-code/sandboxing patterns — low risk, real value on its own even without the rest. M2 (general copy-on-write escrow with full effect-trace capture across shell/file/HTTP/browser, atomic commit/rollback) is where the roadmap's flat cadence misleads: faithfully escrowing arbitrary shell side effects (background processes, daemons, out-of-workspace writes) and diffing 'every path touched, every verb, every egress' is systems engineering on the order of a lightweight sandbox/hypervisor, not a milestone-sized task, and the design's own admission that email/purchases/external POSTs can't be escrowed at all means the hardest-to-build mechanism also has the narrowest domain of applicability (local filesystem/DB/git-backed coding-agent workloads — not browser or API-heavy agents). M4's SMT-backed checker is buildable but likely over-engineered relative to what path/glob/quota checks actually require. Net: a small team can ship a genuinely useful M1-only product quickly; the full vision requires M2, which is the long pole and the part most likely to slip or get scoped down in practice.
keepIdeas: Transcript-independent enforcement as a free variable: putting the permission floor, task delta, and ground-truth ledger in sidecar state that every tool call checks regardless of what's in the context window means compaction aggressiveness stops being a safety risk and becomes a pure cost/quality knob. This is the one move in the design that isn't a straightforward port of an existing pattern (capability security, transactional rollback, and policy-as-code all predate this), and it's adoptable standalone by any harness without building escrow, SMT checking, or macro-execution at all.

Attenuated sub-envelopes for delegation: giving each sub-agent a provably-narrower slice of the parent's envelope (rather than trusting a spawned agent to self-limit, or the parent to hand-write per-delegate rules) is a clean, well-scoped application of capability attenuation to multi-agent delegation. It's far more buildable than general escrow — no shadow-filesystem, no effect-trace capture across heterogeneous tool surfaces, no TOCTOU problem — and it closes a real hole (delegation as an authority-laundering vector) that most current multi-agent setups leave open.

attacks: Enforcement ambiguity, sharpened: the charitable reading is defense-in-depth — the one-time abstract-interpretation proof over a loop body is a fast-path guard, and the concrete per-action Warrant checker still gates every individual effect (coreMechanism literally says 'every primitive effect...passes the fail-closed Warrant checker before it runs'). That reading is coherent and a designer would reach for it immediately. But the doc's own failureModes text forecloses it: it calls checker under-approximation 'the catastrophic case.' Under defense-in-depth, an under-approximation bug just means the concrete checker blocks the action after the proof mis-cleared it — irritating, not catastrophic. It is only catastrophic if the proof REPLACES per-action runtime gating on the compiled fast path (consistent with savesClass's 'per-action concrete checking is the fallback,' i.e. not the default). So the doc's two sections are not merely in tension, one of them (failureModes) settles the question the other section leaves ambiguous, and the answer it settles on is the dangerous one: a single unsound proof can wave 200 actions through at machine speed before anyone notices. That is the same silent-mass-policy-violation failure mode the compaction pitch claims to have eliminated, reappearing with a new root cause (checker soundness instead of transcript drift) exactly where the design claims to be strongest.

The 'floor is never materially negative' claim is chicken-and-egg, not argued. It rests on a triage step correctly identifying which tasks have compilable internal structure BEFORE compiling — but knowing that generally requires exploration, which is precisely why the design's own 200-file walkthrough spends a call exploring 3 representative files before it can propose a Score. So triage is either cheap and uninformed (it will misroute at some unquantified rate, burning the synthesis call the doc admits it 'occasionally' burns) or informed enough to be reliable and is therefore no longer 'one triage call.' The rare-hard-task rubric item survives at all only because of this floor claim, and the floor claim is asserted rather than derived.

Hole under-declaration is not a residual risk (as failureModes frames it) but the central epistemic cost of the minimal-context design, and it directly undercuts the correctness pitch. A transcript-based agent, however bloated, CAN in principle notice 'this conflicts with something three steps upstream' because that context is still visible. A hole call built from only its declared dataflow contract structurally cannot notice an omission in that contract — there is nothing to notice it with. So minimal-context calls convert a class of failure that was at least inspectable (visible in the transcript, if anyone looked) into one that is invisible by construction, backstopped only by whichever acceptance predicates someone thought to write. This is a real trade the design makes for its input-token savings, and the doc doesn't price the trade, it lists it as failure mode #5 alongside four others of clearly lesser severity.

Two unspecified translation/selection steps carry real hidden cost and risk. (a) Per-hole 'relevant Warrant clauses' selection: if it's a deterministic pre-tagged lookup, that's uncosted operator-authoring labor per workspace; if it requires any inference to determine relevance, it's an uncosted token tax on every hole call, eroding the 0.3-3K-token figure the whole cost story leans on. (b) The subset-check itself operates on a formal lattice element, but the model proposes its task Warrant as generated spec text — nothing describes the parser/translator that turns that text into the checked lattice object, and a lossy or ambiguous translation lets the solver correctly prove the wrong thing, silently reopening the self-certification gap the mechanism exists to close.

The rare-hard-task story quietly readmits the recurring-work niche it claims to transcend. Its only first-encounter example (200 homogeneous config files) is valuable because the TASK INSTANCE is internally repetitive, not because it is hard in the sense that matters for this rubric (novel, irreducible, one-off reasoning — e.g. diagnosing an unfamiliar production incident). Its second concrete value story ('second or third repetition, the Score+Warrant pair IS the reusable skill') is explicitly cross-repetition reuse, i.e. the classic recurring-task-amortization niche, just relocated from prompt-injection to runtime retrieval. On the doc's own admission, a genuinely hard, observation-driven, non-repetitive one-off degrades the Score to 'a chain of holes ≈ a normal agent' — the exact case the rubric is asking about gets, by the design's own account, no material benefit.

The abstract-interpretation crux (M4) faces a tradeoff the roadmap doesn't resolve: soundly certifying a loop body over the closed action vocabulary is tractable roughly in proportion to how trivial that vocabulary is (read/regex/write is checkable; anything with data-dependent per-item business logic is not), while the vocabulary's usefulness for real repetitive tasks scales the opposite direction. The roadmap prices this as one milestone alongside four much smaller ones (checker proxy, lattice plumbing, DSL+hole runtime, resumption+eval harness), understating that it is the one milestone that is genuinely open-ended, PL-research-adjacent work rather than integration engineering.

Copy-on-write transactions for 'reversible effect classes' is stated as a clean uniform primitive, but filesystem writes, network API calls, and third-party side effects have entirely different reversibility semantics and each needs its own rollback integration; the M2 milestone folds this heterogeneous, per-effect-type engineering surface into a single deliverable line.

The headline percentages (60-90% input, 30-70% output/calls) are asserted via a plausible narrative, not measured, and the roadmap's own M5 only promises 'demonstrated per-instance, not benchmark-averaged' — i.e. even at the end of the five-milestone roadmap there is no committed plan to produce an averaged, defensible number, despite averaged-sounding numbers being stated up front.

This design's safety core is largely already shipped in this user's own repo: openDaisugi already has an LLM-authored checkable envelope, a Z3-backed verifier that gates each action before it runs, and (per commit history) a call-time gate. That means M1-M2 here are substantially done, which is good for buildability, but it also means the genuinely new content is narrower than the framing suggests: M3-M5 (the Score compiler, loop certification, and disposable-transcript resumption), not the whole five-milestone arc — worth stating plainly since it raises the buildability score and lowers the novelty score simultaneously.
crits.rareTaskVerdict: Real but narrow, and it doesn't reach the case the rubric is asking about. The in-task loop-compilation mechanism genuinely helps large, internally repetitive one-off tasks (200 homogeneous files) without depending on task-type recurrence — that part is a real mechanism, not hand-waving. But it conflates 'big and repetitive' with 'rare and hard.' Its cross-repetition value story is classic recurring-work amortization relocated to the runtime, and its own honest admission is that a genuinely irreducible, observation-driven, one-off hard task degrades to a plain gated reactive agent with no cost benefit — only the (separately real) safety benefit survives. So: works for a real but different niche (batchable one-offs), not for the rubric's target niche (irreducible one-off reasoning-hard tasks).
crits.compactionVerdict: The strongest part of the design, and correctly reasoned: by keeping the Warrant, Score, ledger and checkpoints in a runtime store and reconstructing each model call's context from those artifacts rather than the transcript, there is nothing safety-critical left in the window to lose — this sidesteps rather than merely mitigates compaction risk, and is a genuine structural improvement over transcript-resident policy. It is undercut, though, by the enforcement-path ambiguity: if the compiled fast path substitutes a one-time abstract-interpretation proof for per-action runtime checks (which the doc's failureModes text implies it does), then a checker-soundness bug becomes a new mass-violation failure mode with the same blast radius as the compaction bug it replaces — the root cause moved, the risk of silent bulk policy violation did not disappear.
crits.netTokenVerdict: Partially closes, and the doc deserves credit for engaging the injection-tax question directly rather than ignoring it: retrieving and re-verifying Score+Warrant pairs at the runtime layer instead of injecting them into every prompt is a real, correct answer to the catalog/skill-injection trap. But two costs are left uncosted — per-hole Warrant-clause selection (either uncosted operator-authoring labor or an uncosted inference tax) and Score-authoring/exploration overhead (the triage/exploration calls needed to know a task is compilable at all) — and the net benefit is highly task-shape-dependent, collapsing toward zero on non-repetitive tasks despite being presented with flat percentage ranges that read as broadly applicable.
crits.buildability: Staged and mostly plausible for a small team, unevenly so across milestones. M1 (fail-closed action-gating proxy) and M2 (authority lattice, solver-checked narrowing) are largely already shipped in this user's own openDaisugi (envelope, Z3 verifier, call-time gate), which makes the early roadmap closer to 'wire up existing pieces' than greenfield work. M3 (Score DSL + hole runtime) is a real but bounded engineering lift. M4 — sound abstract interpretation of loop bodies over the action vocabulary, generalized enough to be useful — is the crux of both the headline cost numbers and the strongest correctness claims, and it is open-ended formal-methods-adjacent work whose difficulty trades directly against vocabulary usefulness; treating it as one roadmap line among five is optimistic. CoW transactional rollback across heterogeneous effect types (M2) is also underscoped. Composes cleanly with prompt caching (explicitly, by design) and is compatible in principle with sub-agent and routing architectures, though the 'cheap exploration sub-agent' that seeds Score authoring is itself undetailed.
crits.steelman: By moving the enforcement boundary and all policy state outside the context window — a model-proposed task policy that can only provably narrow a standing operator policy, checked by a deterministic solver rather than the model itself — and by letting genuinely repetitive stretches of a task compile into zero-token deterministic execution instead of one turn per item, CONTINUO could make an agent both cheaper on structured work and safe in a way that a compacted or dropped transcript cannot undermine, because the transcript was never the thing enforcing anything.
keepIdeas: The monotone-narrowing authority lattice, precisely scoped: a model-proposed task policy is admissible only if a solver mechanically proves it's a strict narrowing of a standing, human/operator-authored environment policy — never trusted by the model's own certification. This is the delta worth keeping over a plain per-task envelope-and-verifier (which this user's stack already has): it makes 'the model widened its own authority via clever spec text' structurally unrepresentable rather than merely checked.

Runtime-side retrieval and re-verification of reusable artifacts (Score+Warrant pairs, or more generally any reusable pathway/skill) instead of prompt-injecting them — a direct, independently shippable answer to the skill-catalog input-token tax, decoupled from the entire Score-compiler and abstract-interpretation ambition. Worth checking whether this user's existing 'reusable pathways' already pay an unexamined per-call injection cost that this pattern would remove.

specs.name: Bailiff — the transcript-independent enforcement sidecar (safety-first, honest cost)
specs.thesis: The durable product is a correctness guarantee that survives compaction; cost savings are a bounded by-product of making aggressive compaction and cheap rollback safe — sell the moat, not a multiplier.
specs.coreMechanism: An out-of-process sidecar on the one boundary every harness shares — the tool-call interface. A human-authored FLOOR policy (workspace jail, egress allowlist, destructive-verb lexicon, irreversibility classes) is evaluated by deterministic pattern-matching code on every proposed action, fail-closed. A solver is used in exactly ONE place — proving that a model-proposed per-task narrowing delta is a subset of the floor — not for path/glob checks that ordinary matching decides, answering the critiques that SMT was over-reached. Every mutating action runs copy-on-write (overlayfs/git-worktree) with a PER-AGENT snapshot so parallel sub-agents don't serialize on one lock. A small external progress ledger holds ground-truth workspace state plus a pinned list of active human-stated invariants captured at utterance. Sub-agents are spawned with an attenuated sub-envelope proven ⊆ the parent's, so delegation cannot launder authority (the hole all five inputs left open). Deliberately NO batch compiler and NO reasoning store — those are separate bets that layer on this substrate.
specs.saves: Safety-currency primarily. Cost is claimed honestly and small: (input) safe aggressive compaction with ledger rehydration, ~20-40% prefill on long tasks, bounded because reasoning-trace loss can still force re-derivation — this design does not license compacting deliberation away; (output) cheap rollback removes only the FILE-repair portion of a recovery arc, ~10-20% on failure-heavy tasks — the diagnose/re-plan tokens remain, correcting the 'rollback = no recovery arc' category error. No output-collapse claim. $/token: none directly; it is the substrate that makes Underwriter's routing safe.
specs.correctnessAndCompaction: Authority-independent by construction: the floor is human code, a delta may only tighten it, and the only solver call proves subset — no self-certification anywhere. Fail-closed on unclassifiable action shapes. Compaction: enforcement lives in the sidecar and is evaluated per tool call regardless of transcript contents, so the measured 0%→30-59% violation cliff is structurally impossible. Honest boundary, stated up front rather than in a footnote: this protects the ALLOWED check and human-stated invariants, NOT task rationale or 'right-ness'; in-envelope is not correct.
specs.rareHardTaskHandling: Frequency-independent by construction — floor checks key on ACTION SHAPE over a closed vocabulary, identical on occurrence #1 and #1000, needing no corpus. On a genuinely irreducible one-off (a heisenbug hunt, a novel design), the honest yield is: pre-execution safety on every side-effecting step plus cheap rollback of wrong-but-allowed steps, and zero compilation benefit (admitted). Floor evaluation costs microseconds; a task that never pushes past the floor never triggers delta drafting — a true no-op, never negative ROI.
specs.composition: A pure orthogonal sidecar. Prompt caching: pins a cache-stable ~100-token contract stub. Sub-agents: attenuated sub-envelopes are its distinctive composability win. Routing: it is the blast-radius bound that underwrites Underwriter. RAG: unaffected. It is the substrate the other three bets sit on, and ships valuable alone.
specs.mainRisk: Under-ambition on cost: buyers who want a multiplier may pass over a guarantee, and the honest 'safety only, ~zero cost benefit' admission covers the entire irreducible-one-off class — which is plausibly the modal rare-hard task.
roadmap: M1 — Sidecar + floor: intercept all tool calls; floor as deterministic pattern-matchers; fail-closed on unclassifiable shapes. Exit: a red-team bypass suite shows zero unmediated side effects; measure per-action latency and false-positive refusal rate.

M2 — Narrowing delta + subset solver: admit a model-proposed task delta only on a solver-proved subset relation to the floor; property-test that the composition operator's type makes widening unrepresentable, not merely rejected.

M3 — CoW execution + per-agent snapshot: overlayfs/git-worktree with rollback-retry and NO global lock; measure rollback token cost against the observed file-repair-arc cost on injected-failure tasks.

M4 — Ledger + safe compaction + invariant capture: post-state ledger plus a pinned active-invariant digest re-injected after each compaction; forced-compaction test showing 0% violation with policy fully evicted from context.
M5 — Attenuated sub-envelopes: spawn each child with a provably-narrower slice; test that no child action stream can exceed parent authority, and that parallel children do not serialize.

specs.name: Foreman — agent-declared, blast-radius-proven batch execution
specs.thesis: The token win on internally-repetitive work is not 'write a script' — a competent agent already does that — it is turning an unverified script's unbounded blast radius into a proven one, monetized inside a single instance.
specs.coreMechanism: No anti-unification loop detector (the critiques correctly flagged that as a research problem dressed as a milestone). Instead the AGENT DECLARES a batch: program P, item set I, effect footprint F, acceptance postcondition Q. The sidecar statically analyzes P's write-set, proves F ⊆ envelope BEFORE any iteration (one proof covers all N, so there is no silent mass-violation path), sample-validates Q on k=2-3 items inside a CoW fork, then executes all N under a runtime monitor that kills on first envelope exit, with per-element rollback and fallback to per-item agentic handling on Q-failure. Irreversible tools (send, purchase, external POST) are charter-marked non-batchable and never compiled.
specs.saves: Output-currency primarily, against an HONEST baseline of 'agent writes an unverified script,' not 'agent does N manual turns.' Two real wins: (a) on agents that DO script, the marginal value is converting a machine-speed N-way error into a k-sample catch plus rollback — a safety-shaped but genuine cost avoidance of the debugging arc; (b) on agents that DON'T script, true O(N)→O(1) turn collapse. Per-instance meter: measured cost of the first k manual items × (N−k) versus actual synthesis+verify+apply, replayable single-action mechanism-off (labeled evidence, not a controlled proof, since sampling is stochastic). Input: modest, via fewer turns and less cumulative prefill.
specs.correctnessAndCompaction: Blast radius is proven pre-execution, closing the 'one wrong script executes 200 wrong ops' hole. Honest on self-certification: Q is LLM-authored, so sample-validate-then-generalize is a heuristic, not a proof — explicitly labeled; per-element rollback and transactional apply bound the residual, and irreversible tools are excluded entirely. Compaction-proof because the declared batch is verified against the sidecar envelope, never the transcript.
specs.rareHardTaskHandling: Monetizes a task's INTERNAL repetitiveness on its first-ever occurrence: a novel task touching 200 files pays out on ~193, with the counterfactual computed from this same instance — no corpus. Zero dependence on task-type recurrence. On a non-repetitive task the agent never declares a batch, so the machinery is a no-op. Admitted gap, stated plainly: an irreducible-reasoning one-off with no batch structure gets nothing here — that case is Palimpsest's job.
specs.composition: Layers on Bailiff's envelope and CoW substrate. Caching: the one synthesis call is a stable one-shot. Sub-agents: a child may declare a batch under its attenuated envelope. Routing: the synthesis call goes to a strong model while deterministic execution is free.
specs.mainRisk: The honest baseline shrinks the headline: if competent agents already script, the marginal contribution is 'verified vs unverified script' — real, but a safety-shaped benefit that resists being sold as a large cost multiplier.
roadmap: M1 — Batch-declaration API + static write-set analysis: prove a fixed program's footprint ⊆ envelope; reject on any unprovable write.
M2 — Parametric write-set proof: solver-check programs whose targets are data-dependent; mark irreversible tools non-batchable so they can never enter a batch.
M3 — CoW sample-validation + monitored apply: validate Q on k items in a fork, execute N under a kill-on-envelope-exit monitor with per-element rollback and per-item agentic fallback.
M4 — Per-instance counterfactual meter: measured k-item cost × (N−k) vs synthesis+verify+apply, dual-currency, replayable mechanism-off and labeled as evidence.
M5 — Honest-baseline eval: benchmark against 'agent writes an unverified script' on internally-repetitive one-offs; report the marginal safety and cost delta, not the manual-turn strawman.

specs.name: Palimpsest — a rationale-durable working-memory plane
specs.thesis: On irreducible hard tasks there is no repetition to compile, so the real cost lever is never re-deriving reasoning that compaction dropped — externalize the DELIBERATION, not just the enforcement state.
specs.coreMechanism: A structured external store the runtime writes and reads on the agent's behalf, holding four typed strata: (1) discovered facts with provenance, (2) ruled-out hypotheses and why, (3) open constraints — including mid-task user-stated invariants captured at utterance and, where expressible, PROMOTED into the enforcement envelope (closing the 'don't touch tenant X' gap all five inputs leave open), (4) the current goal/subgoal stack. Compaction then compacts the transcript hard, but each model call's context is RECONSTRUCTED from the store (relevant strata + pinned constraints) rather than the transcript — so 'compact aggressively' becomes actually costless on hard tasks, not merely safe. Writes are cheap structured emissions, not a second prose summarizer, and are provenance-addressed so a dropped caveat is re-pageable verbatim.
specs.saves: Input AND output. Input: aggressive compaction with reconstruction, ~40-70% prefill on long hard tasks — defensible here (unlike the five inputs) because the deliberation the task needs is preserved in the store, not discarded. Output: eliminates the re-derivation tax — re-exploring a ruled-out branch, re-discovering a fact — that pure enforcement-only compaction inflicts on hard tasks, the exact cost the critiques said every other design ignores. Meter: on the same instance, from an identical compaction point, count re-explored branches and re-discovered facts with the store on vs off.
specs.correctnessAndCompaction: This is the compaction-durability bet, extended from enforcement to reasoning. Authority-independence is preserved: facts and hypotheses are the agent's own outputs, so they inform reasoning but NEVER gate actions — the gate stays code+human; only constraint-promotion touches authority, and it flows through the same monotone-narrowing check (a captured invariant can only tighten). Honest boundary: relevance-selection for reconstruction is itself a judgment that can drop the load-bearing stratum — mitigated by verbatim re-page and provenance, not eliminated.
specs.rareHardTaskHandling: This is the bet that targets the modal rare-hard task the others admit they are inert on — deep, singular, non-repetitive reasoning. First-occurrence yield with no corpus: the store fills from THIS task's own exploration and immediately pays back by preventing re-derivation after each compaction. Frequency-independent: payoff is a function of task LENGTH × compaction aggressiveness, not recurrence. No-op floor: a short task that never compacts writes a few cheap records and reads none back.
specs.composition: Complements Bailiff directly — together they make compaction both safe AND costless. RAG: the store is a task-local, provenance-tracked index the retrieval layer can query. Sub-agents: a child returns a fact-stratum DELTA rather than a lossy prose summary, fixing the 'delegate summary is a second un-audited compaction' landmine. Routing: supplies Underwriter's escalation with failure evidence instead of a full transcript.
specs.mainRisk: Relevance-selection for reconstruction is the hard, unglamorous core and can itself become the landmine it exists to defuse; and the per-turn structured-emission tax must stay smaller than the re-derivation it prevents, which is only true on genuinely long tasks.
roadmap: M1 — Typed strata store: facts / ruled-out / open-constraints / goal-stack, provenance-addressed, with a cheap structured-emission hook on the agent loop.
M2 — Context reconstruction: build each call's prompt from relevant strata + pinned constraints instead of the transcript; provide a verbatim re-page API for dropped detail.

M3 — Constraint promotion: capture mid-task user invariants and route the expressible ones into the narrowing gate; run the 'don't touch tenant X' scenario end-to-end under forced compaction and confirm it holds.
M4 — Re-derivation meter: from an identical compaction point on one instance, count re-explored branches and re-discovered facts store-on vs store-off; publish the output-token delta.
M5 — Sub-agent fact-delta return: children return a strata delta, not prose; test caveat-preservation against a summarizer baseline on a task where the caveat is load-bearing.

specs.name: Underwriter — blast-radius-bounded cheap-model routing
specs.thesis: A cheap model is unsafe to trust, not unsafe to CONTAIN — bound its blast radius with an external gate and you can route far more work to it, using gate-rejection and escrow-test failure as authority-independent escalation signals instead of the model's own confidence.
specs.coreMechanism: A cheap model drives envelope-covered steps by default. Every action still transits the external fail-closed gate and CoW escrow. Escalation to a strong model is triggered ONLY by external signals: (a) gate rejection — the cheap model proposed an out-of-envelope action; (b) escrow test/postcondition failure after a shadow run; (c) a structural stop-loss when the same action fails k times. Never by the cheap model's self-report — which is the exact mistake the confidence-gated-effort family makes and this fixes. On escalation the strong model receives failure evidence (Palimpsest strata where present), not the full transcript.
specs.saves: $-per-token currency — the axis the five inputs name only as a composition afterthought. Rough magnitude: 2-5× on price-per-token for envelope-covered steps the gate makes safe to hand to a small model. Per-step input/output are roughly unchanged; the win is model choice made safe rather than reckless. The wasted-cheap-attempt cost on escalated steps is charged honestly against the saving.
specs.correctnessAndCompaction: Authority-independence is the crux and it is clean: the escalation trigger is the external gate/escrow, never the acting model grading itself. No correctness regression — a cheap model's dangerous errors are blocked pre-execution, its wrong-but-safe errors fail visibly in escrow and roll back; worst case is escalation cost = strong-model price plus one wasted cheap attempt. Compaction-durable because the gate that underwrites the routing is transcript-independent.
specs.rareHardTaskHandling: Monetizes per-step difficulty spread within ONE instance — no workload mix and no recurrence needed. A hard one-off still has many easy sub-steps (file reads, mechanical edits) a cheap model can safely drive under the gate, plus a few hard steps that escalate on external failure. Honest failure case: a task that is hard at EVERY step turns cheap attempts into pure waste and nets negative — so a triage cap that skips cheap attempts on high-gate-risk / high-complexity steps, keyed on ACTION STRUCTURE not self-report, is mandatory, not optional.
specs.composition: Rides on Bailiff's gate and escrow as substrate; orthogonal to prompt caching (both apply); complements Foreman (synthesis to a strong model, execution free) and Palimpsest (escalation carries the strata as evidence). It is the cost-multiplier the safety-first substrate deliberately lacks.
specs.mainRisk: The wasted-cheap-attempt tax on hard-at-every-step tasks can invert ROI unless the triage cap is well-calibrated — and calibrating it without a corpus, on novel tasks, is the same cold-start problem the whole exercise is about.
roadmap: M1 — Cheap-by-default routing under the gate with strong-model escalation on gate-rejection only; measure $/token on envelope-covered steps.
M2 — Second external trigger: escrow test / postcondition failure escalates; add the k-failure structural stop-loss.
M3 — Action-structure triage cap: skip cheap attempts on high-gate-risk or high-complexity steps, keyed on shape not self-report; measure the wasted-attempt tax.
M4 — Evidence-scoped escalation: the strong model receives failure evidence (Palimpsest strata if present), not the full transcript; measure escalation prompt size.
M5 — On-instance ROI ledger: net $ with cheap-attempt waste charged honestly; characterize the hard-at-every-step inversion case and the cap threshold that avoids it.

reachedByMany: Move enforcement OUTSIDE the context window and evaluate it at the tool-call boundary, so compaction cannot drop the policy — all 5 designs, the single strongest and most defensible shared claim.
Pre-execution, fail-closed gating: verify before the side effect runs, refuse/escalate on unclassifiable shapes — all 5.
Monotone-narrowing authority lattice: a human-authored floor plus a model-proposed delta that may only TIGHTEN, with the subset relation checked mechanically — no self-certification — all 5.
Copy-on-write / transactional execution with cheap rollback so a wrong-but-allowed action costs a snapshot restore — all 5.

Within-instance program compilation: harvest a single task's INTERNAL repetition into one verified program to collapse O(N) turns to O(1) — all 5 (though the detector-vs-declaration split is where they differ).
An external deed/progress ledger as ground-truth memory that both licenses aggressive compaction and enables per-instance counterfactual metering against a mechanism-off replay — all 5.
Self-gating tiered triage with a no-op floor: microsecond checks for reads, heavy machinery only on risky/batch actions, so trivial tasks pay ~zero — all 5.
oneOffBets: Verification-UNDERWRITTEN aggressive cheap-model routing — bounding blast radius so a small model can be trusted more (PORTCULLIS/Interlock named it, but only as a keep-idea, never a core; promoted here to Underwriter).

synth.note: The five inputs are near-identical instantiations of one architecture (externalized fail-closed gate + within-instance compiler + CoW rollback + monotone-narrowing lattice), so their critiques converged on the same flaws. The synthesis value here is to SPLIT that monolith along its distinct currencies and design-space families into separately-sellable bets — Bailiff (safety-currency + rollback), Foreman (output-collapse), Underwriter ($/token) — rather than one over-claiming stack, and to ADD the bet none of them made: Palimpsest, which targets the irreducible-reasoning rare-hard task every input admitted it was inert on. Shared repairs baked into all four: honest baselines (batch value = 'verified vs unverified script,' not 'N manual turns'); rationale-not-just-state durability (rollback restores disk, not the conversation, so recovery-arc tokens are only partly saved); external-signal escalation instead of confidence self-report; capability attenuation for sub-agents; SMT confined to the subset-proof where it earns its keep; and per-instance counterfactuals labeled as evidence, not controlled proofs, given sampling stochasticity. The four are a composable stack (Bailiff is substrate) but each is a standalone product bet with a different primary thesis and currency — deliberately not variations of one design.
